articles.body: The central idea is Technological ROI : connecting technical investments to measurable business outcomes. Instead of saying, “We need to refactor our monolithic backend,” a technology leader could explain, “Our current architecture delays revenue-generating features by 30%, creating a significant opportunity cost. By modularizing the system, we can recover that capacity and accelerate time to market.” This translation turns a technical “want” into a business “need.” The Strategic Tech Reporting Framework To communicate effectively, technology leaders should use a consistent reporting structure. The Strategic Tech Reporting Framework connects engineering health with business health and gives the board the information needed to make decisions about investment, risk, and growth.

November 20, 2026 · 6 min read · by Iris @ minia2a In the 24 hours to 2026-11-20T09:05Z, our delivery ledger recorded 208 requests that asked a paid endpoint to fetch or inspect a private, reserved, or unresolvable address . They came from 19 external IPs and hit 29 different endpoints. Not one of them booked a strike against a seller. That second half is the part worth writing about. A refusal that lands in the wrong bucket turns a caller's bad input into a seller's outage — and on a pay-per-call marketplace, three of those is enough to delist a healthy service.

articles.title: SLO-based alerting: moving from thresholds to burn rate alerts
articles.excerpt: SLO-based alerting: moving from thresholds to burn rate alerts Threshold-based alerts have a fundamental problem: a 5% error rate at 2 AM with zero traffic looks identical to a 5% error rate during pe…
articles.body: SLO-based alerting: moving from thresholds to burn rate alerts Threshold-based alerts have a fundamental problem: a 5% error rate at 2 AM with zero traffic looks identical to a 5% error rate during peak load. Both fire the same alert. One is nothing, one is a disaster. SLO-based burn rate alerting fixes this by measuring how fast you're depleting your error budget — which makes the severity of a problem proportional to its actual business impact. What SLOs and error budgets mean in practice An SLO (Service Level Objective) is a commitment about reliability. A common one: "99.9% of requests succeed over a rolling 30-day window." That 0.1% tolerance is your error budget — the total amount of failure you're allowed before you've violated the SLO.

articles.title: Your MCP Server Changed Its Tools. Would Your Agent Notice?
articles.excerpt: Many MCP setup examples, including the ones in official client docs, start a local server without a version: "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem", "/Users/me/projects/demo"] Which…
articles.body: Many MCP setup examples, including the ones in official client docs, start a local server without a version: "args" : [ "-y" , "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem" , "/Users/me/projects/demo" ] Which release you get then depends on npx and its cache, not on your config. Cursor's own docs tell you to clear the npm cache and re-add a server to get the latest version. A newer release can offer your agent a different set of tools, and because your config file hasn't changed, nothing looks different on your side. To see what that looks like, this morning I took a snapshot of the tool list from two releases of the official filesystem server and compared them. Below: the script, the real output, what the protocol says, and how Claude Code, Codex and Cursor limit what a new tool can do.

articles.excerpt: Roadside Picnic ends with one of science fiction’s most beautiful lines, a simple wish for happiness that still resonates more than 50 years later.
articles.body: The canon of science-fiction literature is home to countless unforgettable endings, from 1984 ’s short but devastating retrospective ("He loved Big Brother") to The Three-Body Problem ’s defiant reminder that humanity cannot be so easily wiped out. The best sci-fi endings don't offer comfortable closure. Instead, they reframe everything that came before. In their closing lines, great sci-fi novelists leave readers suspended in the aftermath, forced to stew in the terrifying logic of cold technology, the fragility of human nature, and the vast expanse of space.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 19, 2005: Japan's Hayabusa spacecraft makes 1st-ever liftoff from surface of an asteroid
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 19, 2005, the Japanese Hayabusa spacecraft made the first liftoff from an asteroid. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 19, 2005, the Japanese Hayabusa spacecraft made the first liftoff from an asteroid. Hayabusa was supposed to return asteroid samples to Earth. Asteroids are space rocks that were formed during the early solar system. We study asteroids to learn more about the solar system's history. Hayabusa (pronounced HI-uh-BOOS-uh) made two touchdowns on asteroid Itokawa (EE -toh-KA-wah). Each time, the spacecraft went into safe mode. Controllers weren't sure if Hayabusa gathered any material. But they sent the spacecraft back to Earth anyway. Hayabusa's sample return capsule returned to Earth in June 2010 . Scientists found dust of Itokawa inside the capsule, proving that it did indeed capture samples of Itokawa.

articles.body: A new set of slo-mo videos gives us a new perspective on SpaceX's first-ever recovery of a Starship upper stage. The company notched the milestone on Saturday (Nov. 14), when the launch tower at its Starbase site in South Texas caught Starship's Ship spacecraft with its "chopstick" arms. You've probably seen photos and videos showing the epic snag from afar.
